html:
Martin Luther King Jr. was an American Baptist minister who led the nonviolent civil rights movement against racial segregation in the United States from 1955 until he was murdered in 1968.

He was born in Atlanta, Georgia, the son and grandson of preachers, and earned a doctorate in theology in Boston. In the South, Jim Crow laws kept Black people out of white schools, restaurants and bus seats, and kept most from voting.

His work, in brief:

  • 1955 to 1956: as a young pastor in Montgomery, Alabama, he led the bus boycott that began when Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat. It ended with a court ruling against bus segregation.
  • Method: he built a strategy of nonviolent protest and civil disobedience, drawing on Christian teaching and on Gandhi, whose India he visited in 1959 (see King studies Gandhi's methods).
  • 1963: campaigns in Birmingham, where police set dogs and fire hoses on young marchers, and the March on Washington, where he gave his "I Have a Dream" speech at the Lincoln Memorial.
  • 1964: the Civil Rights Act outlawed segregation; King won the Nobel Peace Prize.
  • 1965: the march from Selma to Montgomery helped win the Voting Rights Act.

In his last years he turned to poverty and spoke out against the Vietnam War, which cost him support. He was shot in Memphis on 4 April 1968, where he had gone to back striking sanitation workers. Riots broke out in many cities. A US national holiday honours him every January.
